To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
basic science knowledge and medical reasoning are complementary and that their integration is a dynamic process.

(1) basic science and clinical science are not two different kinds of knowledge, (2) the integration of these two kinds of knowledge can be performed dynamically during the reasoning process and (3) the computational architecture implementing this integration process is the one of a blackboard system.
basic science and clinical reasoning are different in nature, and the integration between them should be dynamic and based on the use of ontologies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of intelligent medical systems based on the integration of basic scientific and clinical knowledge.
the representation, integration, and use of basic science knowledge in the context of medical decision support systems.
the integration of basic scientific knowledge into medical expert systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of a dynamic integration of basic science in clinical reasoning is a promising way of solving many of the current problems of the field of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Medicine, but that further research is needed in order to fully understand its potentialities and limitations.
the basic science knowledge is the necessary condition for the clinical knowledge to be applied in specific cases.
the basic science in medical reasoning is not a static knowledge base, it is an active and dynamic part of the reasoning process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the integration of knowledge from different domains is a matter of the way in which the knowledge is used during the reasoning process, rather than a matter of the representation.
the representation of medical knowledge is not a static task, but an active one, in the sense that the knowledge must be represented and used in the reasoning process.

the integration of basic and clinical knowledge is not only feasible, but that it can also be achieved by using a simple and natural approach, and that this approach is not restricted to the domain of medicine.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the dynamic integration of basic science knowledge in medical reasoning can be achieved by a combination of two main components: an ontology-based representation of the basic science knowledge and a dynamic integration of basic and clinical knowledge during the reasoning process.
the dynamic integration of basic science knowledge and of clinical knowledge is a key issue to improve the performance of intelligent systems in medicine.

the integration between basic science and clinical reasoning should be done in a dynamic manner, and that the computational architecture should be able to represent the different kinds of knowledge in a unified framework, which we call "basic science in medical reasoning".
